utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Doria.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: I remember my learned colleague talking about the period of time that -- in January 1993 as being very cold and a suggestion that the blankets were taken by civilians to protect themselves. So that is why I am putting the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're right. But the question is which blankets actually were put in the cart on which the witness was being transported, because of her injury. So let's proceed and --

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: I thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- at least try to stick to what is relevant to the case anyways.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Madam Stamenic, you also testified having seen those items being taken directly to Srebrenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, which items. It has to be the blankets which are on the cart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it he's referring to the blankets.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The blankets on the cart, an unknown provenance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please answer the question. Are you in a position to confirm that those blankets that you saw in the cart -- not knowing whether they were actually your own or someone else's, were actually taken to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Stamenic. Madam Stamenic, you testified that you saw a person who came into the cell and identified himself as Naser Oric; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Stana Stamenic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He introduced himself as Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Stamenic. Do you recall, apart from the person who came in the cell and introduced himself as Naser Oric, do you recall anyone else coming and identifying himself as Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: Stana Stamenic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Stamenic, you also testified, saying that you saw a man who introduced himself as Zulfo coming into your cell; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Stana Stamenic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall anyone else coming into your cell, apart from the man who introduced himself as Zulfo, coming and introducing himself also as Zulfo?

utterances.speaker: Stana Stamenic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Stamenic, you testified yesterday and today again that a certain man called Ilija and two other males came into your cell bending, bringing firewood for you. Do you recall why they were bending? Do you know why they were bending?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that question was asked by -- it wasn't asked by you when she was referring to that instance, but the same question has been asked by Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Yes. I am coming back on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But then come to the issue. She has already stated that she has no idea why they were bending and whether -- it was put to her that perhaps they were bending over because of the weight of the logs they were supposedly carrying, she said she can't confirm that. So if you have any further question arising out of the cross-examination that could better enlighten us, go ahead. If you don't, move to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Madam Stamenic, do you recall if the men who came bending, who were bending only when they entered into the cell or also when they were going out of the cell?

utterances.speaker: Stana Stamenic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, if we could go to a private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Doria.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Doria. Yes, Mr. Jones, I understand you had one final question that you seek permission to put to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- arising out a point that was made by Mr. Doria. You seek to put the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it needs to be put in private session. There is no objection on our part, that you put this question. But it needs to be put in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Madam Stamenic, we are approaching the end, but there are a few questions that the bench would like to put to you, starting with Judge Hans Henrik Brydensholt who comes from Denmark. He has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Yes. When you were on the stretcher in the prison cell and a man who introduced himself as Naser Oric came to the cell, did he enter the cell? Did he go to where you were placed on the stretcher? Or did he just remain on the door opening?

utterances.speaker: Stana Stamenic [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came up to the stretcher, up to the place where I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: And I understand he asked you, "Why are you in a stretcher?" And do you remember, what did you explain to him?

utterances.speaker: Stana Stamenic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: What did you say? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Stana Stamenic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I had been wounded. He asked me why I was on the stretcher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: And you answered that you had been wounded. Did you tell him, do you remember, that you had been to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: Stana Stamenic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Albin Eser from Germany would like to put some questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: May I start with the question --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: May I start with the question, Mrs. Stamenic following the last question of Judge Brydensholt, how long did the visit of the person who called himself or introduced himself as Naser Oric take? Could you describe how many minutes? Was it short or longer?

utterances.speaker: Stana Stamenic [Resumed]
utterances.text: A short visit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And beside talking about your wounding and whether you got food, did you talk about any other subject while he was in your cell?

utterances.speaker: Stana Stamenic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I would like to go back to the happenings that go along the line. And your testimony in connection with the events is soldiers came to your village and to your house. And you stated -- and I will read it from yesterday's testimony -- that "the soldiers were moving about and so were the civilians. They were loading up things from the house, up on to the ox cart." Now, who was the "they"? "They were loading." Who was loading? Before you mentioned soldiers and civilians. Now, who was loading?

utterances.speaker: Stana Stamenic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, you told us that they were loading, they were taking away blankets and cheese. Now, was there any other food in your house? Or do you know what was the reason why they did only -- took cheese?

utterances.speaker: Stana Stamenic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, with regard to this woman Djemila who told you that you would be exchanged. Did you have the impression that she told you this hope on her own? Or that it was done in some sort of agreement with the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: Stana Stamenic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, you had testified that the evening before you have been exchanged, Zulfo came to your cell and he informed you that you would be exchanged. Now, between your capture and three weeks later when you have been exchanged, were there any information given to you or given any reason why you were captured and that you would, later, be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: Stana Stamenic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The only person who told us anything was Djemila. She told us we would be exchanged. No reasons whatsoever were given to us by anybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So the time between your capture, when you have been informed by Djemila and you were told by Zulfo before the exchange, no reason was given by you why you have been kept in the cell? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Stana Stamenic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, you testified that some of the other women had been taken away and interrogated or at least they have been asked questions. Now, when they came back, did they tell a little bit about what they have been asked? Or would they just come back and keep silent?

utterances.speaker: Stana Stamenic [Resumed]
utterances.text: They returned and they didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Does this mean that while you were in the cell that you had not a lot of talk between each other?

utterances.speaker: Stana Stamenic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: No. But if people are in a cell for such a long time, was there a reason why you did not talk with each other a lot? That you kept silent, as I assume from your answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Or whether they didn't talk a lot. I don't think she said they were silent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: They did not talk a lot, yes.

utterances.speaker: Stana Stamenic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: What do you mean with "no"? I wanted to know what --

utterances.speaker: Stana Stamenic [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't say much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And was there a reason why you did not say much?

utterances.speaker: Stana Stamenic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And what was the reason?

utterances.speaker: Stana Stamenic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Eser. I have got just one final question for you, and then it's over. Madam Stamenic, you've told us how, on one particular day during your stay in the Detention Centre in Srebrenica, a man walked into your cell and identified or introduced himself as Naser Oric. After that day, did you ever see that person again in your life?

utterances.speaker: Stana Stamenic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That brings us to the end of our -- of your testimony. Before you go, I want to make sure, first and foremost, that you have been given all the assistance and attention that you needed to be able to go to where you are now and give testimony. Can you confirm that to me, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I am asking is, I want to make sure that everything has been organised well for you and that you have received all the assistance that you needed so that you could go to where you are now and give testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can also assure you that our staff over there will now, once your testimony is over, give you all the assistance you require to facilitate your return back home at the earliest. On behalf of the Trial Chamber and on behalf of Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser and myself, and also on behalf of the Tribunal, I should like to thank you, Madam Stamenic, for having accepted to give evidence in this trial which the Prosecutor has instituted against Naser Oric. And we also wish you a safe journey back home from where you are. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think we can conclude the videolink and prepare ourselves to usher the next witness. However, I smell in the air some news about this next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes Your Honour I just want to confirm that the next witness has informed us that he will not be using protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: None of the protective measures that we granted earlier on?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, we looked into this yesterday, and as far as I understood it, that in any event, the Prosecution would have -- would have had to apply for protective measures because it was only pre-trial protective measures leading up to the present. We have seen with C-001 and C-007 there is a need to apply for protective measures when the witness testifies. I just wanted to state that understand for the record, because that is our understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, we will see into that and the Prosecution will see into that. I think that your submission is correct. But in any case the question does not arise with this witness any further. In other words, he has agreed to testify without protective measures in place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: That is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, you do not see the utility of us going into closed session for a while, for a minute or two, to have him confirm this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I understand we do not even have a need for even a very short period of closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then let's usher him in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might you give us one minute to change team members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that -- who will be leading this witness, Mr. Di Fazio or yourself?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought so. Yes. I thought so. In fact, here he comes. For the record, Mr. Di Fazio now enters the courtroom, together with Ms. Richardson, while Mr. Doria leaves. Usher, could you please escort the witness in. Mr. Di Fazio, I hope that this witness knows that he will be here for roughly a week or a little bit less than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: He has commitments on the 12th and says that the last day that he can testify is next Monday, but I would think that he would be finished by then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope so. We will see what the situation is and, if necessary, we will split the time equally between you, Prosecution and Defence, and seek to get an undertaking from each of you to finish within the time limit allocated to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please relax. And before I proceed any further, I want to make sure that you are receiving interpretation of what I am saying in English in your own language, or in a language that you can understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, this is something which is of course very important. If at any time, during your testimony here or during the proceedings, there is faulty reception or faulty interpretation or you're not receiving interpretation at all, please draw our attention to that straight away so that we will address it and make sure that everyone is receiving interpretation. Do you understand me? Understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. The other thing that I wanted to have clarified from you is the following: You have -- you would have noticed that so far I have not mentioned your name. And the reason is that sometime back, upon your own request, we had placed, in your favour, some protective measures, some of which -- or practically all of them were meant to hide your identity. We have been informed, this morning, that you no longer seek to have in place these protective measures and that you are willing to testify in open session with no hiding of your identity or withholding of any of your identity any further. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So now I can address you by your name and surname, Mr. Hakija Meholjic. That's you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Good morning to you and welcome to this Tribunal. Very soon you will be starting giving evidence in this case, which the Prosecution has instituted against Naser Oric. Our Rules require that before you start giving evidence, you make a solemn declaration. Unlike in many jurisdictions, we don't have an oath, but we have got something which has the same legal effects. We call it a solemn declaration. It is contained in a piece of paper that has just been handed to you by Madam Usher. Our request is that you read out that declaration aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal that, in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truly, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to make yourself comfortable and feel relaxed. If at any time you need a break, please tell us so, and we will give you a break. We usually have a break every hour and a half. Since you are starting now, the next break will roughly be in 45 minutes' time from now. But as I said, should you require us to stop for a while, please let us know. The first to go will be Mr. Di Fazio, who you have met already. He will put to you a series ever questions which I kindly ask you to answer as fully as possible and as truthfully as possible, in conformity with the oath that you have just taken. He will be followed later on by Madam Vidovic, who is lead counsel defending Mr. Naser Oric, and again your responsibility, in terms of your oath, is to answer their questions equally, fully, and truthfully. You have absolutely no right to draw or to make any distinctions between questions coming from the Prosecutor -- Prosecution and questions coming from the Defence. Each side has the right to put questions and you have an obligation under oath now to answer those questions truthfully and honestly to the best of your ability. Did I make myself clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. One final thing is that you will be testifying here for a number of days. I wish to make it clear to you that there is an absolute prohibition on you to discuss the merits of your testimony with anyone outside this courtroom. In other words, during breaks or between sittings and between sessions, you're not allowed to discuss the merits of your testimony with anyone. That includes, also, over the phone with relatives or friends that you might try to talk to over the days. Have I made myself clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. The other thing, if in the course of your testimony you wish to bring to the notice of the Trial Chamber anything, please feel free to do so. We are here to make sure that you begin and finish your testimony without -- with the least interruptions and without any interference. All right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jones -- sorry, Mr. Di Fazio. Your turn will come later, Mr. Jones. Let me first clear this up with the witness. Witness, I understand that you would like to be back home by a certain day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must go home Tuesday a week, at the latest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So today a week? So I am tasking the Prosecution to liaise with the Victims and Witnesses' Unit, with a view to making sure that if we finish on Monday, the witness can find himself back home on Tuesday. Because I don't know if there are any flights available on Monday and we need to verify that and make certain that there are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. I understood that the witness is happy to -- oh, if -- perhaps we should be clear about this. Does he need to actually fly back on the on Monday? Or could he fly back on the Tuesday? Because I understood he could fly back on the Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The way I have understood it is that he can stay here Tuesday. That's how I have understood it, but ... Yes, Mr. Meholjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must be in Bosnia on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He must be in Bosnia on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I don't know on Tuesday of next week what time we are sitting, whether we're sitting in the morning or whether we're sitting in the afternoon. In any case, it will be safer to mark time Monday as the last day of his testimony and only exceptionally go beyond that. But in any case, in a way that would ensure a return to his country by Tuesday at the latest. So I am tasking you with that, addressing you, Mr. Di Fazio, because you will be leading this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I will undertake to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can lead the witness on the initial questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Meholjic, I think you were born on the 7th of April, 1949. You are of Muslim ethnicity. You're married, and you've got two children. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just on the issue of your testimony here, I can inform you that on the 21st of October 2004, this Trial Chamber issued an order that you be subpoenaed and attend at -- to this court to testify. Can you tell the Trial Chamber if in fact you were served with a subpoena on the fifth of November last year at a location in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And you are here to testify in answer to that court order? You have to answer, because your words are recorded and it becomes part of the transcript. So just let us know, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Continuing your personal background. You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, before you continue. For the record, the subpoena was issued, for the record, because the witness showed reluctance to come forward and testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to make it clear that he is here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. He was unwilling to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Unwilling to come but has met his obligation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But we must make it clear that the subpoena was issued not capriciously but because there was an intimation from his side that he was unwilling to come forward and testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: There is no question about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's move. Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Continuing your personal details, you've had over 20 years' experience as a police officer. I'm talking about the period of time prior to the outbreak of war in 1992.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: 1989 you were appointed the chief of police for the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Well, I tend to say commander instead of chief. I would call my position the sector commander. You're saying the chief of police, but we had the area divided into different sectors and in the area of Srebrenica, the municipality of Srebrenica, there were several sectors and so there was more than one person in charge of individual sectors and I was in charge of the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. And a year later -- sorry. My apologies. About a year after the war started in Bosnia, around the 26th of April, 1993, you were appointed as the commander of police or chief of police, whatever is the appropriate expression, for the Srebrenica municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And who appointed you to that position?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: It followed a proposal from the Presidency an I was appointed by the minister of the interior Bakir Alispahic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. The proposal -- you said a proposal from the Presidency. Which Presidency are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: The municipality of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And following your appointment to that position, can you tell us who was appointed as your subordinate commander of uniformed police?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: No one. I was superior. I was the chief of police and we had three sectors there. One, the uniformed police led by a commander, and then there was the crime squad, and then administrative and legal affairs, that was the third department. And the person in charge of administrative staff was also in charge of issuing documents, IDs, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Di Fazio. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a mistake in interpretation. The witness was asked about his superior, but -- no, his deputy and it was interpreted as superior. And therefore the witness might have been confused. But my impression now is that the witness has actually understood the question properly and so that's why I wanted to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't think it is the case of rectifying anything. Do you have any questions? It's all right. Let's proceed. I thank you Madam Vidovic. I got the same impression too, actually and Judge Eser at the same time was fully aware of what was going on at the same time. Proceed, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Let me approach it this way: Do you know a gentleman named Tajib Mustovic?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Following your appointment as chief or commander of police in April of 1993, did he play any role in the police hierarchy; if so, what was it?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: The commander of uniformed police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Subordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And do you know a gentleman named Rasid Efendic?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did he play any role in the hierarchy of police and, if so, what was that role?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did have a role. He was the chief of the crime squad.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was he subordinate to you?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you remain holding that position as commander or chief of police for Srebrenica municipality until the fall of Srebrenica in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Prior to the outbreak of war in April of 1992, had you been a member of any political party or parties? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the communist league of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And did you join any other parties in the period of time closer to 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Have you ever -- do you know of a party called the social democratic party? SDP?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Have you ever had any connections with that party?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: I am a member -- no, there must be a mistake. He first said SDA and now it looks like SDP, so it's the SDP that you're talking about. I am indeed a member of the SDP in Bosnia-Herzegovina and I'm a member of its highest body, that is to say the main council of the board of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. I'm sorry if I -- if I made a mistake. I thought I said SDP, but in any event, I just want to know a bit more about that, your connections with that political party, the SDP. Were you a member of that party in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know a gentleman named Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber approximately how long you've known him.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps -- I don't know what you mean. I met him perhaps three or four years before the start of the war and then since then, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you this. Throughout the years 1992 to 1995, that period of time, did you have dealings with him on numerous occasions?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "numerous occasions," but we did have contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Turning to the period of time prior to the outbreak of war in April of 1992. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what his position was, if you know, in the Srebrenica area. What position did he hold?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: I've told you that in case of crisis situations every municipality in the system back then was divided into war police stations, which were divided into and distributed across local communities. And Naser was the commander of the reserve police station at Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you know how long he held that position, and the period of time in which he held that position?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: I've told you that when there is a crisis situation, that is to say an actual disaster or a risk of war, that was the usual approach. And in such a situation, reserve police stations are set up, or rather war police stations manned by reservists, and they could be there when there was a crisis situation, in much the same way as I was. I can't really remember the date, but when there was a crisis, yes, that's when it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Moments ago you said that Naser was the commander of the reserve police station at Potocari. During what period of time was Naser the commander of the reserve police station at Potocari? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: When the crisis or rather the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, perhaps five or six months, I can't really tell you exactly. I don't remember. But until the outbreak, or rather until the 17th of April, that's when everything fell apart. And there was nothing left. The 17th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can I -- do I understand your answer to be that you believe that Mr. Oric was the commander of the reserve police station at Potocari for a period of about five or six months preceding April 17, 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes. But maybe a shorter period of time as well. As of the moment when the chief of police issued the order for that to be set up, for that body to be set up, that's when it happened. Nothing else. I can't really remember the time scale. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In that period of time leading up to the outbreak of war, April of 1992, did you have any social dealings with Mr. Oric? Or did you just know of him as a professional colleague?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Well, Naser is younger than I am, livelier. He had his friends, I had my friends. We were colleagues. But we didn't go out together. I mean, he was not married and I was a married man, so we're talking about different lifestyles as it were. And he was there for a short period of time. Too short in order for us to be able to spend time together socially, but we did have a good relationship, yes. We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I want you to turn your attention now to the structure of the police in Srebrenica municipality prior to the outbreak of war in April of 1992. First of all, can you tell the Trial Chamber who was the overall chief of police or commander of police for the Srebrenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Hamed Salihovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And who was next down from him?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Mustafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And at that -- I've already asked you about Tajib Mustafic in 1993, but at that time prior to the outbreak of war in April 1992, what was his official position?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: He was a commander, the commander of the uniformed police. He held the position in 1993, but also before the outbreak of the war he was our commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks for that clarification. You've already touched upon this subject, namely the sectors. Was Srebrenica municipality divided up into various sectors? Police sectors I mean.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: What I'm going to say -- well, please don't take it as the whole truth. I'm just going to explain what I'm trying to say. We had 19 local communities. As to whether we had 19 war police stations or how many, I can't tell you. But the municipality was divided into many of these local communities and there were quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And one such sector was the sector -- I'm talking about the pre-war period, pre-April 1992 -- the one such sector was the Srebrenica town?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And you were the commander or the chief of police, whatever is the appropriate expression, for that sector, Srebrenica town, prior to the outbreak of war?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the -- of any sector that might have encompassed Potocari?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: I think it was Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You earlier mentioned that he was the -- he was in charge of reserve police. Do I take it, from your answer, that he was also in charge of uniform police for the sector of Potocari?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: I must clarify a couple of things. Unfortunately, well, I've come here to tell the truth and I'm going to tell the truth. But you have to give me some space. I have to be able to explain things properly. We did not have all that many police officers, we had very few of them, in fact. So if you think in terms of 19 local communities and two people per community, I mean we don't -- simply did not have that many professional police officers. So for the most part, those police stations were manned by reservists, perhaps one or two professional police officers, depending on the police station, but Naser was professional. And the second man would be a reservist and the same applied to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. That's a good clarification. Thank you for that. Can I ask you now to turn to events at the very outbreak of war. And I don't want to dwell too long on this particular topic. On the 17th of April, 1992, are you aware of Serb forces or Serbs in the Bratunac area issuing any sort of ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: To whom was that ultimatum issued?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: To us, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Where was the ultimatum issued and to which particular individuals was the ultimatum issued?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: To the president of the municipality. I believe that his name was Besim Ibisevic. His last name was Ibisevic. I'm not sure about his first name. I believe that it was Besim. Also, it was issued to Dr. Saber Begic and to Alija Hasic on behalf of the police station. In Bratunac, it was issued to the Fontana hotel, where the talks were held, and the ultimatum was given to us saying that by 18 of April, at 8.00 in the morning, the Muslims should hand over their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a few more details on this -- on this matter. I take it you -- I take it you weren't present when this ultimatum was issued, it's something that you learnt of later?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The three men that you mentioned, the president of the municipality and Dr. Begic and Mr. Hasic, they comprised the delegation that went to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And it's your understanding that there, in Bratunac, they received this ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did they return to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And following their return, was there a meeting held in Srebrenica to discuss this issue of the issuance of the ultimatum by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And was the ultimatum explained at the meeting? The nature of the ultimatum, what it was, what was required?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Shall I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You can, but just before you do, I would like you to tell the Trial Chamber, can you recall who was present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't need everybody's name, but the names you can remember, the more important personalities and figures, who were there.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether there were any prominent persons there. There was myself. Hamed Salihovic, Alija Hasic, Nurija Porobic, Suljo Hasanovic, Tajib Mustafic, Jusuf Halilovic. There was also the president of the municipality. Dr. Sabit Begic was there. There may have been somebody else, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell us how the meeting progressed, what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: The president of the municipality informed us of the fact that the delegation had been invited to come to Bratunac by the JNA and the SDS, and that the ultimatum had been given to us, to the Muslim forces, although we did not have any forces at that time, that we should hand over our weapons by 8.00 in the morning of the 18th, which was the following day. As far as I knew -- first of all I was surprised that I was at the meeting, because I was not a member of the municipality, but at the meeting I realised that there were no weapons to speak of. What we had was in the police station. In the police station we had light weapons, Serbs, Muslims, Croats, the Roma had their personal weapons such as pistols and batons. It was not the police station that distributed arms to the members of the police of only one nation. Those were the distributed to the reservists and to the active officers alike. In the former system the police was in charge of protecting the leaves and the property of citizens. Whereas the JNA was there to defend Yugoslavia and not to shoot at their own people. If they indeed considered these people to be their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you for that background detail, but it is not exactly what I'm seeking. I wanted to know how the meeting progressed and any decisions that were taken regarding weaponry in particular. The background political undercurrents and details are not a matter I need trouble you with, okay? The facts, as they say; could you tell us how the meeting progressed.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: This was also a fact. But let me move to the meeting itself. The Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. chief of the police station, Mr. Hamed Salihovic, to my great surprise, said only this, and I will quote; I remember it well. He said that he was speechless. This man Mustafic, who was my commander, asked if anybody could guarantee his life if he surrendered his weapons. And then Dr. Sabic said, who could guarantee that. Suljo Hasanovic interfered and said he was not prepared to hand over his pistol. We laughed at that. The situation was difficult, and this sounded like a joke. Then they asked me whether I would surrender my weapons and I said, "no."

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just pause there. Explain to the Trial Chamber, when these men at the meeting said -- asked you will you hand over your weapons, what precisely did you understand them to be referring to? A shotgun back home? Or weapons in a police station? What weapons are you -- did you understand them to be speaking about?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: To the weapons that was held at the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Continue. And how did you react to that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: My suggestion was that we should go to the woods, to organise people for defence and I said, "I am not surrendering my weapon. For as long as I have my piece I'm safe." In Bratunac they had already started stopping people and killing people, and we drew from that experience, and that's why I said I would not surrender my weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was there any final decision taken by the assembled men at this meeting regarding the issue of any weaponry or regarding any response to be given to the Serb forces concerning the ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Nothing was concluded. Everybody fled Srebrenica. They left people to their own means.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And following the meeting, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: After the meeting, I went to the temporary police station, which was in the hunters' hall, where that police station was temporarily located at.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's in, somewhere -- in Srebrenica town itself?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is that the place called Lovac?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And police weaponry, normal police weaponry for day-to-day police activities, was that located there?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you see or meet anyone at Lovac?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw some people. I told them that Srebrenica had surrendered and I told them that if they wanted to, they could go to the woods or go back home, as they wished.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Oric that day?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: At Lovac?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a discrete topic in itself; would this be an appropriate moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. We will have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Now, before the break, we got to the point where you -- you told us about your decision to go up to Lovac where the weapons were located, the police station there, and that you met Mr. Oric. Tell the Trial Chamber what passed between you, what did you discuss.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Oric came to me sometime in the afternoon or early evening. He told me that there was nobody for him to approach, that Salihovic, the head of the police, passed through Potocari and told them "everything is over. You do whatever, and you all go your own way." He came to ask me what I would do. I suppose that he did not go to Suceska. He did not talk to anybody else. He came to Srebrenica and I told him that I decided to go to the woods and see what would happen. And then he said to me: "What if you surrender your weapons and you -- and the -- Srebrenica fell?" I said that I wouldn't do that. So we said that we would both go to the woods. Some people had fled. Very few people were left in his police station and in mine. There were no communications. The repeater no longer existed. The municipality powers no longer existed. He went to Potocari. I went to the woods in the evening with 56 other men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he give you any information as to what he intended to do in that situation?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: No. He didn't know. I was not sure that he wouldn't leave. Nobody knew anything. I was not his subordinate. He was not mine. This was just a conversation of two men who were at the equal footing. We were powerless. The police had fallen apart. The people were left to their own means. We were -- it was not up to us to comfort the people. We had to take our own destiny into our own hands. We were left to our own means. We he can changed opinions on everything. And finally, we concluded that we would go to the woods and see what would happen. And if we could, we wanted to go to Tuzla. And if not, we would see what would happen. This is how I remember things. I believe that I said that there is a rock in Potocari called Majdan, and from that rock you could see well what was going on on the road. We were just a handful of people who had been issued an ultimatum by a huge force. We had to see what we could do. And everybody had their own views, and that's how he left. And we finally decided that maybe we would see each other. He decided to remain in the area of Potocari. I will remain in the area of Srebrenica. And then we would see how things went.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. So in answer to my question, did he give you any information as to what he intended to do in that situation, your answer is - do I understand you correctly - that he told you he was going to remain in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he tell you what he was going to do in Potocari, what his plans were there?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: We did not have any plans. We had to adapt to the situation. We just wanted to see how the situation would go. Most of the people believed that this foolish situation would come to an end within 15 days or so. There was nothing specific. We were not prepared for anything. There was nobody in charge to lead us or to plan anything. We were left to our own means.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So you and Mr. Oric parted ways on -- on that day?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, the 56 men that you had, were they all police officers?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Some reserve policemen fled, together with the rest of the people and there were some other people who wanted to join the reserve police. Nobody wanted to take weapons or anything. And during those five or six days of crisis, they were given the weapons, those who wanted to become reserve policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So in answer to my question, do I understand you to be saying that the 56 men comprised policemen and aspiring reserve policemen. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. What sort of weaponry did you have when you -- did you and these 56 men have?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: I had an automatic rifle made in Yugoslavia. There was also an RAP, which is a combat set. I also had a pistol. This is what I had. And I also had a machine-gun, M53. I had four PMs, which is somewhat lighter than a classical machine-gun. I also had 18 automatic rifles. When I said "I had," I mean the people who were with me. And I also had some semi-automatic rifles. And there may have been some make-shift rifles that people constructed themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you and the group then leave Lovac and head up into the hills and the forests around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: There were Serbs in Srebrenica. And I said that in the evening we would turn on the lights in the -- Lovac and we would exit through the back door and head towards the woods. And this is what we did. We left the lights on in Lovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, it's not -- I don't think it is in dispute, that you spent a period of time with your men out in the forests and the hills and the area around Potocari. Did you eventually return to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Just a correction here. I was not around Potocari. I was around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That was my mistake. My apologies. You're quite right. But it's not in dispute that you spent - I don't think - that you spent some time in the area of the forest and hills around Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just tell the Trial Chamber, when did you eventually make your way back to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: I returned to Srebrenica at the beginning of the second half of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to talk to you briefly about that period of time between your taking to the hills, so to speak, and your eventual return in the second half of May into the town itself. Was Srebrenica shelled during that particular time?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: On the night when we took to the woods, it was snowing. We were not prepared for that. We didn't have any tents. We slept under the trees. On the following day, on the 18th at half past one, the shelling of Srebrenica started; actually, the parts of Srebrenica which were populated by Muslims. In front of the house of Blasko, whose last name I don't know, Blasko and his mother shelled Srebrenica From the place called Kapura, above their house. Kapura, K-a-p-u-r-a, is the name of that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What I would like you to do is to try to give the judges an overview of what you saw and heard happening in Srebrenica during that period of time. Now in so far as shelling is concerned, can you tell Their Honours, was it a daily occurrence or did it only occur once, or was it intermittent in the period of time between your taking to the hills and your return to Srebrenica. I want the Trial Chamber to get a picture of the shelling. I don't need each day-by-day description, but just an overall picture of what you saw and observed in so far as shelling is concerned.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: On the 18th, Srebrenica was shelled. Some of the population of Srebrenica, Bosniaks, remained in the town. Later on, the White Eagles came and Arkan's men also came. They planted, they beat people up and killed them. And we were observing all of that. We thought that maybe we should do something about that. However, during the night we would meet by the white mosque in Srebrenica. We met with a Serb called Slobodan Zekic, also known as Zes [phoen]; he was a colleague of ours. He told us what had been going on in Srebrenica during the day. We couldn't see that, although we could see a lot of things. People were being killed. Houses were being torched. And we thought that maybe we could conquer them militarily. However, the population was still prepared to suffer. They didn't want to leave the place. We could storm the town and do something. However, the stronger forces would come and they would chase us out. The population told us not to do that until the 6th of May. On the 29th of April, 1992, my house was torched together with a number of other houses. I knew that I should not reply, that I shouldn't respond to that. I wanted the war to be over. However, there is some people who wanted to defend their houses, which was absurd at the time. The Ustic family wanted to defend their house. They didn't want to see their house being torched. On the 6th of April Goran Zekic took a group of people who wanted to torch houses and they --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just pause there, sorry. First of all the date, the 6th of April in relation to Mr. Goran Zekic. Are you correct there? Or is it another date? April?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: I know what you're asking me, but we will come to that. Goran Zekic was not killed then. This was on the 6th of May when the nephew of Akif Ustic, whose name was Muamer, was killed. I believe that his last name was Cengic. There was a clash taking place. They wanted to take the old town of Srebrenica, the all the walls that sour owned a cluster of houses. We call that the Old Town, Stari Grad. The Serb forces wanted to take that. The Ustics put up resistance together with some other people. And Mohammed [as interpreted] was killed. After that, some Serbs also got killed. I don't know how many. After that, shelling started and so on. Some two days later, I believe, we were informed by Slobodan Zekic that Goran Zekic had been seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now just tell the Trial Chamber who Goran Zekic is; just a sentence or two will suffice.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Goran Zekic was the president of SDS at Srebrenica. He was a member of their highest executive body, within the SDS, I don't know what it's called, the main board or whatever. But anyway, the most important body. Before the war, unfortunately, he was a judge at the municipal court in Srebrenica. He was one of the Chetnik leaders. A Chetnik duke. And we once had a meeting, him and myself and he insisted we have that meeting. And he explained to me that the war was unavoidable and that his mother had asked him not to become a war criminal. He lost his life very early on, so I don't know whether he would have become a war criminal or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I'm trying to keep silent as much as I can. But if we go on like this, this witness will be here for two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, I know. I will try and make sure that the -- it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are two options either you control him yourself or I control him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. I will do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, I address you. I do understand that many witnesses come here and want to tell us the whole story, and I do appreciate the fact that many witnesses wish to do this, because it's also important for the history of the events. However, my suggestion to you is that you try to answer the question that is put to you, the whole question, but nothing but the question. Don't go beyond. Because you will be here for weeks and not for days. And you won't be able to leave here on Monday or on Tuesday. Please try to answer only the questions that are put to you. If you go beyond that, and we don't stop you, you will be here forever. Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So, what I would like to know is, following the death of this Mr. Goran Zekic, in an ambush, did the Serb forces eventually leave Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: After Goran Zekic's death, they set fire to some people in their houses and then they left Srebrenica. When I say "some people," I mean Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And did you re-enter Srebrenica some time later?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Approximately when?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: I've told you. In beginning of the second half of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And did you went with these 56 men that you've spoken about?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: One less. No, no. I don't remember exactly, but there were not as many people as all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, where did the 56 men who were - sorry the 55, now - 55 men who were with you go upon your re-entering Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: We entered Srebrenica in the evening and we all went to our homes. I went to my father's home since my home was no longer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you know a place called the Domavija hotel?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did any of your men take up residence there?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Not that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But in the days that followed, did they take up residence there and did you also work out of that place?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: At a later stage we all stayed there and that's where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And about what period of time would you say it was that you and your men took up residence there, at the -- by the -- at the Domavija hotel?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: 24 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. But about when following your return to Srebrenica? Was it a day, or two, or three; or was it months later? Or did you slowly gradually start to put your men in that particular place?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: A couple of days later, two, three, four days later. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Thanks. Do you know a place call Bajramovici?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: About how far is it from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, perhaps five kilometres, something like that. That's if you take the road. And as the crow flies, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you at some point of time become aware of there having been a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. meeting at that particular place?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: I did not find out about the meeting being held, but I did find out once it had been held.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And, yes, okay. I understand that. Thank you. So I take it you did not attend any meeting at Bajramovici?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When did you find out about this meeting at Bajramovici, was it after your return to Srebrenica? Or was it while you were still up in the hills and in the forests around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Upon our return to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know a gentleman named Asim Tepic?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Tell the Trial Chamber what you first heard had transpired at this meeting at Bajramovici.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: When I got to Srebrenica and when I got to my parents' house, Asim Tepic, who was my neighbour, came to see us that evening and he told me that staff for the Territorial Defence was elected and that Naser was appointed as commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Were you asked to go anywhere?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: They -- after Asim told me that I had to go to Domavija hotel and talk to Naser and Ahmetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can I get the full name of Ametic, please, what's that gentleman's name?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Asim Tepic. Asim Tepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Did you in fact go to the Domavija hotel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I want to clarify this for sure. Your previous question was the following: "Okay were you asked to go anywhere?" And then he said "they, after Asim told me that I had to go to the Domavija hotel, and talk to Naser and Ahmetic," and then you ask him; "Can I get the full name of Ahmetic, please." What's that gentleman's name and he said: "Asim Tepic." I don't think you were talking of the same person. Because if you ask him for Ahmetic, it can't be Asim Tepic. That's a different person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's right. Thank you. Yes, I'm grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what we need to know from you is Ahmetic's name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Akif Ustic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Akif Ustic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, did you go to the Domavija hotel?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did this Asim Tepic, your neighbour, did he participate in the meeting? Or was he just the man who brought you the message?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: He just brought me the message.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And who was at the Domavija hotel when you went there?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: I went with Amir Kulaglic and Halidam Delic [phoen], and at an office there I found Akif Ustic and Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you know what the meeting was to be about before you went?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: I didn't know. How could I know what we were going to talk about? Presumably the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And about how long after your return to Srebrenica did this meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: I think on the day after.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Did Mr. Oric speak to you?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: At first Ustic addressed me, and then Naser participated in the conversation later as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. What did they say to you?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Akif told me about Naser being appointed as commander and he himself as deputy commander, and that I was told that I should be disarmed because I wasn't doing my job properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You've already mentioned a meeting held at Bajramovici. Was it explained to you, at this meeting, that there had been a previous meeting at Bajramovici, where this election had taken place? That's what I would like to know.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: No. Asim Tepic told me, and I was simply told by them about their own situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did they, did they provide you with anything more specific other than that you should be disarmed because you weren't doing your job properly? For example, did they say they wanted all the weaponry of your men or ... What exactly did they -- did they say to you?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Mainly Akif was leading the whole conversation and he said that we should be disarmed. And when he said that, I replied "I have nothing to say to you," and I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did Mr. Oric express any opinions at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Well, he said that, yes, we had to do our job, but Akif wasn't allowing for certain things to be done in a certain way. I think he was upset because of his cousin's death.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who was upset?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Akif.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What was the reaction when you made it clear that you weren't going to comply with them, with what they wanted?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: No. Nothing. I just left the meeting. And there was no reaction on their part.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was there any conclusion or agreement reached between you all?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Not on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know a gentleman named Zulfo Tursunovic?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was he present on this occasion, or not?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Following the meeting, you'd been informed that Mr. Oric was the commander of the -- sorry, it's gone off the screen. Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment. Can you be a little more specific. When you said that Mr. Oric was -- it was made known to you that Mr. Oric had been elected the commander, did anyone explain to you or did you have any understanding as to what he was the commander of?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Territorial Defence of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you recall, can you tell the Trial Chamber if that expression was used during this encounter with Mr. Oric and Mr. Ustic? "Territorial Defence." "Territorial Defence of Srebrenica," do you remember that actually being used during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Akif opened the meeting and he informed me that Naser was elected commander and he himself deputy commander, and it went without saying that it was the Territorial Defence. I don't know what else. I mean, I don't really recall whether anyone mentioned the term, but I do know - on that occasion - but I do know that later on the term was being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Your evidence has been that the meeting was inconclusive. Nothing was decided. Did you return to your men and to the Domavija hotel?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you discuss what had transpired at the meeting with anyone?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Everyone. I held a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just -- let's be precise. When you say "everyone" who do you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: Everyone. I mean, you asked whether I talked to my men. I did talk to all of my men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay, thanks. All right. And what did you say to them?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: I told them that things were not going well. I informed them about the situation, about the fact that some leadership had been elected. I did not know about any of the names, any of the people. And I said that the meeting was a difficult one and I told them what Ahim said. And we decided that we would not relinquish our arms and that, if necessary, we would continue through the woods in the direction of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, briefly tell the Trial Chamber why it was that you didn't accept the election of Mr. Oric to this position that you have described.

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: At the first meeting, nobody asked whether I agreed or not. It was an attack on the part of Akif against me, against me as a person and my men as well. And I've mentioned already, I mean on that day, on the 6th of April, no, on the 6th of May --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "I made a mistake," says the speaker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- his cousin was killed and he basically accused me or blamed me for not providing any assistance. And that was my fault. And if you ask a personal question, well, I can answer it. I mean, there was no course of that sort at that particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't really think that that answers your question, Mr. Di Fazio, but it is up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you leave that meeting agreeing, either openly or in your own mind, to accept Mr. Oric as the commander of the TO, or not?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, tell the Trial Chamber why. Why didn't you accept it? He'd been elected, at this meeting in Bajramovici, as the commander of the TO, why did you not accept that?

utterances.speaker: HAKIJA MEHOLJIC
utterances.text: It was one of the reasons. It was a complex time, and I thought that Naser was young and that the entire situation in that area at the time, that it was something that would likely prove very difficult for a young and inexperienced person to deal with and to grapple with the problems we had to grapple with. And I was against it for that reason. No other reasons. No personal reasons or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where do you stand? Because we have already gone past quarter to two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. I can -- we can stop here. That's not a problem. I can finish this off tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Meholjic we are going to stop here for today. We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. In the meantime try to rest and come prepared so that you can then keep your questions to the -- what is just necessary so that we will do our best to make sure that you go back home by Tuesday. I would like you, Madam Vidovic, Mr. Jones, and you, Mr. Di Fazio, to meet between now and tomorrow morning and agree on how you are going to split the time this witness will be in the box between now and Monday, end of the sitting on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And if it is the case of proceeding on Tuesday, that's assuming that the sitting is also in the morning. Monday it's definitely in the morning. I think Tuesday it is as well. But I want to make sure that he would be in a position to return back home on Tuesday if he is still testifying here on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I am tasking you with -- sitting down together and trying to agree on how you are going to split the time between you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: We've already had a preliminary conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. But I would like it finalised. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 6th day of April, 2005 at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
